 These are reasons for the decision in the appeals of GholamXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (the principal appellant), his wife, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, their three sons, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX and XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (the "appellants"), all citizens of Iran, from departure orders issued against them at Vancouver, British Columbia, on September 30, 1998. The departure orders were issued on the basis that the appellants were described in paragraph 27(1)(b) of the Immigration Act, 
1976, ("Act "),1 namely, that the appellants were granted landing subject to certain terms and conditions which were not complied with. At the outset, counsel for the parties agreed that the appeals on behalf of all the appellants be joined and heard together. Th e appeals were joined and heard together. THE ISSUES
 The issues to be resolved are: (a) whether the removal orders are valid in law; and (b) whether, having regard to all the circumstances of the case, the appellants should not be removed from Canada. THE EVIDENCE
 The principal appellant was landed in Canada on July 18, 1995 as an entrepreneur. His landing was subject to terms and conditions that within a period of two years of his landing, the principal appellant was to establish, purchase or make a substantial investment in a business or commercial venture within Canada. The purchase or investment was to make a significant contribution to the Canadian economy. It was to create employment opportunity in Canada for one or more Canadian citizens or residents other than the 
 
1 R.S.C. 1985, c.I-2, as amended. 
1999 CanLII 14712 (CA IRB)
 - 2 - V98-03664 V98-03665 V98-03666 V98-03667 V98-03668
 
 
 principal appellant and his dependents. The principal appellant's wife and their three sons were also granted landing at the same time as the principal appellant as dependents of the principal appellant. Their landing was also subject to the same terms and conditions as the principal appellant. The appellant testified that prior to 1992, he worked in the textile industry for ten years as a selling and purchasing agent. The appellant's father owned and operated a production plant which produced weaving threads used in making carpets. In 1992, the appellant's father was deceased and the principal appellant allegedly inherited his father's production plant. In early 1995, the principal appellant and his family came to Canada as visitors. The principal appellant's brother-in-law is a permanent resident of Canada and allegedly deals with new business entrepreneurs from Iran. Th e principal appellant, after discussion with his brother-in-law, decided to apply for permanent residence in Canada as an entrepreneur. A visa officer at the Canadian embassy in Bonn, Germany, interviewed the principal appellant. The principal appellant, his wife and their three sons were issued immigrant visas. The principal appellant was apprised of the terms and conditions of his landing. The principal appellant testified that at the time of his landing, he was aware of the terms and conditions subject to which he was granted landing. The evidence indicates that after the principal appellant's landing, he found the labour costs in Canada too high and abandoned the idea of textile finishing for which he was issused a visa.
2 On September 15, 1996, the principal ap pellant wrote a letter to the Canada Immigration Centre, Vancouver, and enclosed an application to vary or cancel the terms and conditions Of landing.
3 In support of his application, the principal appellant provided information in regard to his investment of $170,000 in a company, S.E.S. Fire Seal

 Industries Ltd., which was contemplating the manufacturing of a fire stop device. The evidence indicates that the S.E.S. Fire Seal Industries Ltd. was incorporated on June 13, 1995, prior to the appellants' landing in Canada. On September 11, 1996, the S.E.S. Fire Seal Industries Ltd. issued 1200 class A shares, 17% of the company shares, to the principal appellant. The $170,000 of the principal appellant's investment enabled the company to buy property from Mr. XXXXXXXXXX, a relative of the appellant. In the meantime, the principal appellant continued running his businesses in Iran. Ms. XXXX, an immigration officer, in a statutory declaration,
4 dated January 15, 1998, avers that she did not receive any eviden ce which would have made her decide to cancel the terms and conditions of landing. On September 22, 1997, the principal appellant wrote to Ms. XXXX that the company S.E.S. Fire Seal Industries Ltd. was totally insolvent.
5 The principal appellant, however, was reimbursed for most of his investment of $170,000. The principal appellant's letter continues to state that the appellant's counsel, Mr. XXXXXXX, was a director of the S.E.S. Fire Seal Industries Ltd. and acted as his consultant and representative. The letter further states: By late October, early November 1996, Mr. XXXXXXX had failed to raise the required capital to permit S.E.S. FIRESEAL INDUSTRIES Ltd. to get off the ground and as all funds had been depleted, Mr. XXXXXXX conveniently resigned his position. Although some of the other directors tried to keep the company alive, by January of 1997 the company was totally insolvent to the extent that not only their telephone lines were disconnected, but gas and electrical power to their unit was also shut off. I understand that not only were you kept in the dark about the above events, but also attempts were made to present a going concern to you. For this I 
 
4 Exhibit 12 to the inquiry held on July 27, 1998, p. 17. 
5 Exhibit c-12 to the inquiry held on July 27, 1998, p. 88.

 apologise and hope you realise that this was done without my knowledge and against my wishes. Since January Mr. XXXXXX has endeavoured to resurrect this project and has recently met with some success. Firstly that S.E.S. FIRESIDE INDUSTRIES Ltd. was able to return the plant that it occupied to the original owner. This enabled the management of S.E.S. FIRESEAL INDUSTRIES Ltd. to return the bulk of my investment to me. Secondly Mr. XXXXXX has been able to acquire substantial investment capital to implement his project. I have been assured by Mr. XXXXXX that should I reinvest this capital in his company (S.E.S. Ent. Ltd.), that he wi ll be able to bring my case to a successful conclusion. I have therefore decided to embark on this venture and have appointed Mr. XXXXXX as my representative. At the hearing, however, the principal appellant testified that the information in this letter is not truthful and Mr. XXXXXX wanted the principal appellant to be part of a fraud. The principal appellant admitted that he did not market any products manufactured by the S.E.S. Fire Seal Industries Ltd. He has no employee at present. He allegedly intends to employ at least one person in the future. On December 18, 1997, Ms. XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, an immigration officer interviewed the principal appellant. Ms. XXXXXXXXX, in her statutory declaration, dated December 19, 1997, avers that the principal appellant told her that he was a travelling man and was not prepared to remain in Canada to run a business. His children had been residing in Iran for nine months at that time. He allegedly has not been able to dispose of his assets in Iran. At the hearing, the appellant testified that soon after his arrival in Canada, he started an import-export company by the name of IRCA. In early, 1996, IRCA allegedly imported a container of oriental carpets. A letter, dated July 24, 1998, from the Big 8 Management states that the principal appellant is one of the shareholders and vice-president of IRCA Enterprises Ltd. and has 
1999 CanLII 14712 (CA IRB)
 - 5 - V98-03664 V98-03665 V98-03666 V98-03667 V98-03668
 
 
 been active in this company since the date of corporation registration on February 1, 1995.6 However, a letter written two days earlier, on July 22, 1998, on the letterhead of the Royal Bank of Canada indicates that the principal appellant was the President of IRCA. The letter goes on to state that IRCA had operated an account with the Royal Bank since April 1995, three months prior to the principal appellant's landing in Canada. The appellant's mother, his three sisters and one brother are all residents of Iran. The appellant testified that during the last four years he has spent approximately two and one half years in Canada. ANALYSIS
 The Appeal Division, pursuant to subsection 73(1) of the Act
, may dispose of an appeal made pursuant to section 70: (a) by allowing it; (b) by dismissing it; (c) in the case of an appeal pursu ant to paragraph 70(1)(b), respecting a removal order, by directing that the execution of the order be stayed. The exercise of discretion must be consistent with the objectives of the Act.
 One such objective is set out in paragraph 3(i) which recognizes the need to maintain and protect the health, safety and good order of the Canadian society. The Appeal Division's task is to balance the safety and good order of the Canadian society against every extenuating circumstance in favour of the appellants. The evidence indicates that the principal appellant was unable to comply with the terms and conditions subject to which he and four other members of his family were landed. Despite immigration officer XXXXXXXX's request to provide her evidence in regard to S.E.S. 
 
6 Exhibit A-1. 
1999 CanLII 14712 (CA IRB)
 - 6 - V98-03664 V98-03665 V98-03666 V98-03667 V98-03668
 
 
 Fire Seal Industries Ltd., the principal appellant failed to provide any evidence which would have satisfied her of the principal appellant's compliance with the terms and conditions of his landing. There is, moreover, no evidence that the principal appellant participated actively and on an on-going basis in the management of S.E.S. Fire Seal Industries Ltd. The principal appellant apparently continued to spend most of his time and energy with his textile company in Iran. The appellant testified that soon after his landing in Canada, he realized that the labour costs in Canada were too high for him to engage in textile finishing business here. There is no evidence that the appellant approached the Canadian immigration authorities during the first year of his landing in Canada in regard to his intention not to engage in the type of business for which he was issued a visa. Mr. Justice XXXXXXXXX in Chan
7 wrote: When the immigrant lands, the immi gration officer at the port of entry attaches conditions to the immigrant's visa which incorporate the representations the immigrant made to th e visa officer. In this way, the representations survive the landing and the immigrant can be required to fulfil his or her representations, failing which, he or she may be held to have breached the conditions attached to the landing and may be removed. On September 1996, more than one year after the principal appellant's landing in Canada, he submitted an application to cancel terms and conditions of his landing. The application was accompanied by extensive information apparently intended to create the appearance of a thriving enterprise. However, when the immigration officer, Ms. XXXX, asked for specific supporting evidence, none was provided. 
 
7 Chan, XXXXXXX v. M.E.I. (F.C.T.D., [1994] 2 F.C. 612 (T.D.); no. 92-T-1825), Rothstein, May 12, 1994. 
1999 CanLII 14712 (CA IRB)
 - 7 - V98-03664 V98-03665 V98-03666 V98-03667 V98-03668
 
 
 In the principal appellant's letter, date d September 22, 1997, he acknowledged that S.E.S. Fire Seal Industries Ltd. never got off of the ground because of a failure to raise the required capital. The bulk of the principal appellant's capital was returned to him because the potential production site was returned to the original owner, a relative of the principal appellant. The principal appellant never had any significant involvement in the management of the S.E.S. Fire Seal Industries Ltd. It is hard to believe that a company that never got off of the ground could have made any significant contribution to the Canadian economy. Nor is their any credible evidence that employment opportunities of any significance were ever created in Canada. There is no evidence that the principal appe llant, during his interviews with the two immigration officers, Ms. XXXX and Ms. XXXXXXXXXX, on October 17, 1996 and December 18, 1997, respectively, provided any information regarding his involvement with IRCA. Moreover, the principal appellant was landed as an entrepreneur and not as an investor. There is a significant difference between the two categories. The evidence indicates that the principal appellant is described in paragraph 27(1)(b) of the Act
 because he knowingly breached the terms and conditions subject to which he was granted landing. The other appellants, similarly, are described in paragraph 27(1)(b) of the Act
 as they too failed to comply with the terms and conditions of their landing. It has been more than four years since the appellants were landed in Canada. They have been in breach of the terms and conditions of their landing during this time. There is very little evidence in support of their ever complying with the terms and conditions of their landing in the future. Except for the principal appellant's brother-in-law and a distant relative, Mr. XXXX, the appellants' have no other close relatives in Canada who would suffer dislocation in the event of their removal. Most of the close relatives of the appellants are residents of Iran. The 
1999 CanLII 14712 (CA IRB)
 - 8 - V98-03664 V98-03665 V98-03666 V98-03667 V98-03668
 
 
 principal appellant, since his landing in Canada, has continued to operate his textile business in Iran. Based on all the evidence, I do not find sufficient grounds have been established, under all the circumstances of the case, that would warrant the granting of special relief under the Appeal Division's discretionary jurisdiction. The removal orders issued against the appellants are valid in law. The appeals of GholaXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX and XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX are dismissed pursuant to paragraph 73(1)(b) of the Act
. ORDER
 The Appeal Division orders that the appeals be dismissed
. The removal orders made the 30th day of September, 1998 is in accordance with the law, and the appellants have failed to show that, having regard to all the circumstances of the case, the appellants should not be removed from Canada. “XXXXXXXXXXXX” XXXXXXXXXXXX 
 Dated at Vancouver, B.C. this 13 day of December, 1999. 
You have the right under ss. 82.1(1) of the Immigration Act to apply for a judicial review of this decision, with leave of a judge of the Federal Court - Trial Division. You may wish to consult with counsel immediately as your time for applying for leave is limited under that section.
